title: File Handling and Filesystem
goal: Read and write files safely, check that a stream opened, and use std::filesystem for paths.

topics.title: Write a file with ofstream
topics.body: `std::ofstream` creates or truncates a file. Always test `is_open()`: a failed open leaves the stream unusable and every later write silently does nothing.

topics.title: Read line by line
topics.body: `std::getline` returns a stream reference that converts to false at end of file, so the loop reads until the file is exhausted.

topics.title: filesystem checks a path
topics.body: `std::filesystem::exists` and `file_size` need `<filesystem>`. They make file handling explicit instead of relying on a failed open.

debug.title: Reading without checking the open
debug.error: Wrong output: [] — the stream never opened, and reading it produced an empty result instead of an error.

debug.title: ofstream used without fstream
debug.error: error: variable ‘std::ofstream out’ has initializer but incomplete type

tasks.title: Count the lines in a file
tasks.statement: Write two lines to a file, then read it back and print the line count.

interviewBank.q: Why check is_open instead of assuming the file exists?
interviewBank.answer: Opening can fail for permissions, a missing directory or a locked file, and a failed stream stays in a failed state. Reading it yields nothing, so the program continues with empty data unless the open is checked.

interviewBank.q: What is the difference between a text and a binary stream?
interviewBank.answer: A text stream may translate line endings, while a binary stream reads and writes the bytes exactly. Use binary for serialized structures, images or anything whose bytes must round-trip unchanged.

defenseBank.q: A file-based feature works locally and fails in production. What do you check?
defenseBank.answer: The working directory, permissions and whether the path is relative to a location that exists on the server. A relative path resolves against the process cwd, which differs between environments.
steps: Print the absolute path being opened.
Check permissions and the directory's existence.
Prefer a configured absolute path over a relative one.

defenseBank.q: Why is std::filesystem preferred to manual string paths?
defenseBank.answer: It handles separators, joins and existence checks portably, so the code does not depend on the host's path syntax. Manual concatenation breaks on the platform you did not test.

mini.title: Contact book on disk
mini.brief: Write three name lines to a file, read them back and print them numbered.
steps: Open an ofstream and check it.
Write the three names.
Read with getline and print a counter beside each.

lab.title: CSV report
lab.brief: Write a three-row CSV with a header, read it back and print the number of data rows.
milestones: Read the first line separately as a header.

title: Modern C++ and Version Evolution
goal: Use the features that changed everyday C++: auto, nullptr, range-for, optional, structured bindings and constexpr.

topics.title: auto and nullptr
topics.body: `auto` deduces from the initializer; `nullptr` is a typed null pointer constant, unlike `NULL` which is an integer. Overload resolution can tell them apart.

topics.title: Range-for and structured bindings
topics.body: `for (const auto& [key, value] : map)` names both halves of a pair without `first` and `second`, which makes loops over maps readable.

topics.title: optional models absence
topics.body: `std::optional<T>` either holds a value or holds nothing, which is clearer than a sentinel. Check it before use; `value()` throws when empty.

debug.title: value() on an empty optional
debug.error: the program failed at runtime (exit null) — terminate called after throwing an instance of 'std::bad_optional_access'

debug.title: constexpr initialized from a runtime value
debug.error: error: the value of ‘n’ is not usable in a constant expression

tasks.title: Optional fallback
tasks.statement: Return std::nullopt from a function and print the value_or fallback.

interviewBank.q: Why is nullptr better than NULL?
interviewBank.answer: `nullptr` has its own type, so it converts to any pointer type without becoming an integer. `NULL` is usually 0, which can select an int overload and hide a bug.

interviewBank.q: When should a function return optional instead of a pointer?
interviewBank.answer: When absence is a normal outcome and the value is small or cheap to move. A pointer suggests an object already exists somewhere; optional suggests the function may produce one or none.

defenseBank.q: How do you decide which C++ standard a project targets?
defenseBank.answer: By the compiler support the deployment actually has and the features the code needs, not by the newest standard. Pin the flag, test it in CI and document the requirement.
steps: Check the compiler's supported standards.
List the features the code relies on.
Pin the standard flag and state it in the README.

defenseBank.q: Why label C++23 and C++26 features explicitly?
defenseBank.answer: Support varies by compiler version, so a feature that compiles locally can fail elsewhere. The label tells the reader which flag and which compiler were verified.

mini.title: Modern rewrite
mini.brief: Rewrite a loop with auto, nullptr and a structured binding over a map, then print the same result as the original.
steps: Write the traditional version.
Rewrite it with modern features.
Print both results and compare.

lab.title: Standard probe
lab.brief: Print __cplusplus, use a C++17 feature and a C++20 feature, and state what the numbers mean.
milestones: Use structured bindings and if constexpr.
Explain the flag that produced the value.

title: Data Structures and Algorithms
goal: Analyse complexity, implement core algorithms, and choose a data structure from the operations the problem needs.

topics.title: Big O describes growth
topics.body: Big O counts how work grows with input, ignoring constants: a linear scan is O(n), a halving search is O(log n). Two algorithms can both be correct and differ by orders of magnitude at size.

topics.title: Binary search halves the range
topics.body: On a sorted array, compare with the middle and discard the half that cannot contain the target. The loop runs O(log n) times; the overflow-safe midpoint is `lo + (hi - lo) / 2`.

topics.title: Dynamic programming remembers
topics.body: Tabulation stores each subproblem once, turning an exponential recursion into a linear pass. The array is the memory of answers already computed.

debug.title: A binary search boundary that skips the last element
debug.error: Wrong output: -1 — `lo < hi` exits before checking the last remaining element.

debug.title: Recursion without a base case
debug.error: the program failed at runtime (exit null)

tasks.title: Binary search index
tasks.statement: Search for 7 in {1,3,5,7,9} with binary search and print the index.

interviewBank.q: How do you choose between a hash map and a balanced tree?
interviewBank.answer: A hash map gives average constant lookup but no ordering. A balanced tree gives O(log n) lookup with sorted iteration and range queries. Choose by whether order is part of the problem.

interviewBank.q: What is the difference between O(n log n) and O(n)?
interviewBank.answer: A linear pass touches each element once; a sort-based solution does logarithmic work per element. At a million elements the difference is a factor of about twenty.

defenseBank.q: How do you explain an algorithm's complexity in an interview?
defenseBank.answer: Name the operation that dominates, count how many times it runs as a function of n, and state the space the algorithm needs beyond its input.
steps: Identify the nested or repeated operation.
Express its count in terms of n.
State the auxiliary space.

defenseBank.q: Why start with brute force before optimizing?
defenseBank.answer: It proves you understand the problem and gives a correct baseline to test the faster version against. The optimization then has a reference answer and a measured reason.

mini.title: Two pointers
mini.brief: Given a sorted array, find whether two values sum to a target using two pointers.
steps: Start one index at each end.
Move the left index up or the right index down by comparison.
Stop when the indices meet.

lab.title: Sorting comparison
lab.brief: Implement bubble sort and use std::sort on the same array, and compare the number of comparisons each performs.

title: Multithreading and Concurrency
goal: Start and join a thread, protect shared data with a mutex, and know why a data race is undefined behaviour.

topics.title: A thread must be joined or detached
topics.body: `std::thread` starts running immediately. Its destructor terminates the program unless the thread was joined or detached first.

topics.title: A mutex serialises access
topics.body: Two threads incrementing the same counter race unless the read-modify-write is protected. `std::lock_guard` locks on construction and unlocks on destruction, including on exceptions.

topics.title: atomic for a single value
topics.body: `std::atomic<int>` makes one read-modify-write indivisible without a mutex. It does not make a whole data structure thread-safe.

debug.title: A thread destroyed without join
debug.error: the program failed at runtime (exit null) — terminate called without an active exception

debug.title: Joining the same thread twice
debug.error: the program failed at runtime (exit null) — terminate called after throwing an instance of 'std::system_error'

tasks.title: Worker thread sum
tasks.statement: Run a lambda on a thread that sets a value to 21, join it and print double the value.

interviewBank.answer: Two threads access the same memory, at least one writes, and there is no synchronisation ordering them. In C++ that is undefined behaviour, not just an unexpected value.

interviewBank.q: Why is a mutex not a complete concurrency design?
interviewBank.answer: It keeps one critical section correct but introduces contention and deadlock risk, and it does not make a compound operation across several calls atomic. The design has to define the invariant and which lock owns it.

defenseBank.q: How do you prevent deadlock between two mutexes?
defenseBank.answer: Always acquire them in the same global order, or lock both at once with std::scoped_lock, which uses a deadlock-avoiding algorithm.
steps: List the locks a thread takes.
Impose one order on every path.
Prefer scoped_lock when both are needed together.

defenseBank.q: Why does a race sometimes pass tests?
defenseBank.answer: Its outcome depends on timing, so a run on one machine can happen to serialise the accesses. Passing once says nothing; the absence of synchronisation is the bug.

mini.title: Safe counter
mini.brief: Increment one shared counter from two threads with a mutex and print the exact total.
steps: Wrap the increment in a lock_guard.
Start two threads with the same lambda.
Join both and print the counter.

lab.title: Race demonstration
lab.brief: Run the same increment loop with and without a mutex, and explain the difference in the final value.
milestones: Run the unprotected version several times.
Explain why only the second is guaranteed.

title: Professional Engineering and Testing
goal: Structure a project, assert what the code promises, and use the compiler's warnings and sanitizers as tools.

topics.title: The standard you compiled with
topics.body: `__cplusplus` reports the language standard the compiler used. If it prints 201703, the build is C++17; a modern feature compiled without the right flag fails here first.

topics.title: assert states a precondition
topics.body: `assert` checks a condition in debug builds and is removed with NDEBUG. It documents what must be true and fails loudly instead of corrupting data.

topics.title: static_assert checks at compile time
topics.body: `static_assert` runs during compilation, so a violated assumption stops the build with your message. It is the cheapest test to run and the hardest to skip.

debug.title: A static_assert that fails
debug.error: error: static assertion failed: int must be 2 bytes

debug.title: A tested invariant that is false
debug.error: the program failed at runtime (exit null) — main: main.cpp:7: int main(): Assertion `add(2, 3) == 5' failed.

tasks.title: Assert the contract
tasks.statement: Write add(a, b) and assert that add(2, 3) is 5, then print passed.

interviewBank.q: What is the difference between assert and an exception?
interviewBank.answer: An assertion documents an internal precondition that should never be false and is removed in release builds. An exception reports a runtime failure that callers are expected to handle, such as invalid input.

They surface uninitialised reads, unused results, narrowing conversions and non-standard extensions before they become runtime bugs. A warning-clean build is cheaper than finding the same defect in production.

defenseBank.q: How do you structure a small C++ project?
defenseBank.answer: Headers declare the interfaces, one source file per implementation, and a build file lists the targets. Keep main thin so the logic can be tested without it.
steps: Separate declarations from definitions.
Keep one responsibility per translation unit.
Put the executable's entry point in its own file.

defenseBank.q: What does the One Definition Rule forbid?
defenseBank.answer: Two different definitions of the same function or object in one program. Declarations can repeat, definitions cannot, which is why headers hold declarations and source files hold bodies.

mini.title: Warning-clean build
mini.brief: Compile a small program with -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic, fix every warning and show the clean rebuild.
steps: Compile with the three warning flags.
Read each warning and fix the cause.
Rebuild and show an empty warning list.

lab.title: Sanitizer run
lab.brief: Run a program with an out-of-bounds read under AddressSanitizer and read the report.
milestones: Identify the allocation and the access in the report.

title: Projects, Design Patterns and Career
goal: Assemble the course into a portfolio project, apply a pattern where it earns its place, and explain your code in an interview.

topics.title: A project is a set of responsibilities
topics.body: Split a console application into input, domain rules and storage. Each part can then be tested and replaced without rewriting the others.

topics.title: Singleton only when one instance is the rule
topics.body: A private constructor plus a static accessor enforces one instance. Use it for a genuinely singular resource; otherwise it becomes hidden global state that tests cannot replace.

topics.title: Two pointers in an interview
topics.body: A sorted pair-sum uses one index at each end: move the left up when the sum is too small, the right down when it is too large. Linear time, constant extra space.

debug.title: A singleton that can be copied
debug.error: Wrong output: 0 — the copy is a different object, so the class no longer has one instance.

debug.title: A private constructor called from main
debug.error: error: ‘constexpr Config::Config()’ is private within this context

tasks.title: Sorted pair sum
tasks.statement: Use two pointers on {1,2,4,7} to decide whether any pair sums to 9, and print the boolean.

interviewBank.q: How do you present a project in a 5-minute interview?
interviewBank.answer: Problem, constraints, the one design decision that mattered, the result with a number, and one thing you would change. The rest belongs in the repository README.

interviewBank.q: When is a design pattern unnecessary complexity?
interviewBank.answer: When there is only one implementation and no sign of a second: a factory for one type or an observer with one listener adds indirection without a decision to make. Patterns pay for variation.

defenseBank.q: Why is Singleton criticised despite being common?
defenseBank.answer: It is global state with a constructor, so tests cannot substitute it and dependencies are hidden. A passed-in object with an interface gives the same single instance without the coupling.
steps: Name the hidden dependency.
Show the test that cannot isolate it.
Replace it with an injected instance.

defenseBank.q: What makes a C++ portfolio project credible?
defenseBank.answer: It builds with one documented command, has tests for the core rules, handles bad input and explains its trade-offs. A small finished project beats a large half-written one.

mini.title: Roster report
mini.brief: Build a small roster report with a struct, a loop and an average, and print the count and average.
steps: Store the records in a vector.
Accumulate the marks.
Print the count and the integer average.

lab.title: Capstone plan
lab.brief: Write the README for a console project: problem, features, build command, test plan and one trade-off.
milestones: State the problem in two sentences.
List the build and test commands.
